question: Is plucking the eyebrows forbidden for women, or are there exceptions to the hadith cursing it?
asked: How do we understand the hadith prohibiting the plucking of the eyebrows, and the fact that Allah's curse is on this? Is there any exception to this rule?
answer:
This question, I'm actually going to spend a good amount of time discussing it, not because of the issue itself, but we're going to use this as a case study, because it's very important that we understand some of the reasons why our scholars differ. And so today I will actually be going into a lot of detail to demonstrate the fact that different scholars have different ways of approaching the tradition. And inshaAllah, whichever position that you follow, there should be an understanding and an acceptance and a respect and a tolerance for other opinions out there.

The hadith in question is a hadith that is narrated by Ibn Mas'ud radiAllahu ta'ala 'anhu, and it is reported in Bukhari and Muslim. It is a much longer hadith, but the key phrase in it is that Ibn Mas'ud reported that the Prophet ﷺ cursed: la'ana Rasulullah ﷺ al-washimat wal-mustawshimat wal-namisat wal-mutanammisat. That the Prophet ﷺ cursed the ladies that put on markings or tattoos, and the ones that ask for these tattoos to be put on, and the ones who, an-namisat (we'll just translate it for now as the plucking of the eyebrows; we're going to come back to this translation), wal-mutanammisat, those ladies that ask for their eyebrows to be plucked; those that change the creation of Allah, al-mughayyirat khalq Allah, they're changing the creation of Allah.

And the la'na, or the curse, has been mentioned in this case from the Prophet ﷺ, la'ana Rasulullah, and then it has also been narrated la'ana Allahu, Allah Himself has cursed. So both of these narrations are found, and it is an authentic hadith because it is mentioned in the Sahihayn.

Now, as I said, today I'm actually going to go into quite a lot of detail, because I really want to use this as a case study, so that we broaden our horizons and so that we understand why and how our scholars have looked at these texts, and why there is a spectrum of opinion. In a nutshell (and again, I'm being a little bit simplistic for now) we see that there are different ways, or paradigms, to look at these traditions. And we can say, for the purposes of our talk today, that we can categorize the scholars who looked at this tradition into two categories.

The first category were those who took it at face value, who took it at its literal value, and they didn't really think about the causes or the concerns or the reasons behind this tradition. And they simply took this (and that's a valid paradigm) and they applied it without any conditions, without any circumstance. It is applied unconditionally across the board. And this is the position that is well known, and you will find this very common on most Q&A websites that answer Islamic questions, and other scholars that are well established on social media and well known. It's very common to hear this position that it is completely unconditional and there are no exceptions.

And at the same time, you have another group of scholars from the beginning of time who looked at these traditions and they tried to understand: well, what is the cause, or what is the reason, such that we will apply this hadith when that cause exists? When the reason is the same, we will apply that hadith. But when the reason does not exist, then maybe the hadith, or the ruling narrated in this hadith, is not going to apply.

And in fact, you see this tension, you see these two different paradigms, even from the beginning of time. In fact, you see it in the famous incident of the Sahaba themselves, when the Prophet ﷺ told the Sahaba to pray Salat al-'Asr in the lands of the Banu Qurayzah. Now, this is a very interesting hadith that really demonstrates this. I don't want to call it tension, because the Sahaba did not quite have a tension amongst them; there wasn't an actual tension between them, there was a tension of understanding. And it's a very, very eye-opening episode in the lifetime of the Prophet ﷺ that demonstrates that texts can be understood differently, and that the question of how literal do you want to be, or how rational do you want to be, is actually a very natural tension. There's nothing un-Islamic, there's nothing modernistic, there's nothing that goes against our iman in Allah and His Messenger. Both of these camps equally believe in Allah and His Messenger, and we find them amongst the Sahaba.

Now, what is this story? And it is a very important story. The incident is that the same day that Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala miraculously caused the confederates to scatter helter-skelter (the army of the confederates, the Battle of the Ahzab; as you know, that sandstorm came), the morning that they woke up and they prayed Salat al-Fajr, lo and behold, the entire camps have cleared. 10,000 have disappeared, mashaAllah, tabarakAllah, because Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala has miraculously sent the winds and caused them to disperse. So the Sahaba came back elated, overjoyed, and they took their armor off and they went back home. After one month of a siege, obviously they need to relax, they need to recover, they need to recuperate.

Now Jibreel came to the Prophet ﷺ and he said to the Prophet ﷺ, "If you have taken your armor off, realize the angels have not taken their armors off. We still have to deal with the treachery of the Banu Qurayzah." Now, there was a treacherous incident: they betrayed the Muslims, backstabbed the Muslims, and they needed to be dealt with. Had it not been for the miracle of Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala, the treachery of the Banu Qurayzah might have been fatal for the entire community. So those traitors have to be dealt with. So Jibreel came and said to the Prophet ﷺ, "We have not taken our armors off. We have to deal with those people."

And therefore the Prophet ﷺ wore his armor again, and he went out and he prayed Salat al-Dhuhr. Keep the chronology in mind: he prayed the Dhuhr prayer, and he announced to the gathering that basically, hurry up, go back home, change into your military gear again, and then hasten to get to the lands of the Banu Qurayzah, which was around two hours, let's say, a walk from the masjid of the Prophet ﷺ. And he gave that command: "None of you should pray the 'Asr prayer until you get to the Banu Qurayzah."

Okay, you understand what's going on. He's prayed Dhuhr ﷺ, and he's basically saying: get to Banu Qurayzah before Salat al-Maghrib. I want you to pray your 'Asr there. Do not pray 'Asr with me, do not pray 'Asr in your homes. Get back home, hasten up, arm yourself back, get onto your camels and your horses, and march to the Banu Qurayzah, the goal being you arrive there before Salat al-Maghrib. So you will pray 'Asr in Banu Qurayzah, and then we will deal with the traitors.

Now, the announcement was made, and it caused a little bit of a panic and chaos. People have to go home and tell their families and pack, and everything has to happen. So the Prophet ﷺ immediately left. He's ready, he's already put his armor on. He and his entourage ﷺ have left, and they're going to get to the Banu Qurayzah way before the rest, and he's waiting for the rest of them to come.

Now what happens? The batch that leaves, they leave too late. They weren't able to get ready, they weren't prepared, it took a while. I mean, it's understandable. And so by the time they leave, it's already past 'Asr time, and they're going towards the Banu Qurayzah, and the sun is about to set, and they're not going to catch the 'Asr salah if they delay it all the way to the Banu Qurayzah.

So understand what's going on here. Let me give you a hypothetical example. Suppose the sunset was at 6pm, let's say, and they would arrive at 7pm. It's already 5:30, and there is no way that they're going to be able to pray 'Asr unless they delay it. So now they have a clash. What should they do? Should they take the verbatim, literal meaning of the hadith, "Do not pray 'Asr until you reach Banu Qurayzah," and so they will watch the sun set, and they will not stop for salah, and they will allow the 'Asr to become qada', because the Prophet ﷺ said, "Do not pray 'Asr until you get to Banu Qurayzah"? Or do they understand the rationale? Do they understand that what was intended was to hurry up and to make haste and to try to get there before 'Asr? Now that we were not able to do that, well then obviously we should pray 'Asr now, and then we'll pray Maghrib when we get to the Banu Qurayzah.

You understand the two scenarios, I hope, inshaAllah. Once again, the issue is: how literal do you want to be? Do you want to take it at face value, or will you understand the rationale, and then, where the rationale does not exist, you will not apply the ruling?

So the Sahaba began to talk amongst themselves. One group said, "He said we should only pray 'Asr in Banu Qurayzah. Therefore we're not going to pray Salat al-'Asr right now. We're going to watch the sun set, and we have the opportunity to pray, but we are obeying the Messenger, and we're going to get there, and we will pray 'Asr after Maghrib time. We're going to pray 'Asr and then we're going to pray Maghrib." And the other group said, "No, but that's not the intent, that's not the goal, that's not the point of saying this. There is a rationale, and now that that rationale is not being met, we're supposed to pray 'Asr and then work our way there."

Guess what happened. The Sahaba could not figure out amongst themselves one united plan. And therefore some groups of people decided to not pray 'Asr, and they continued marching onwards, delaying 'Asr until after Maghrib. And another group, they stopped and they prayed 'Asr right then and there, and they finished 'Asr and they prayed it on time, and then they marched onwards. When both groups arrived, the Prophet ﷺ rebuked neither of them. He did not make this an issue. It was not something that was a big deal: "Oh my God, you guys are following the Sunnah against the Sunnah." No, the both of them tried their best, and the both of them examined the tradition, and they reached different views.

Now, this same, if you like, tension in terms of understanding the text, it has trickled down to many of our rulings as well. The same philosophy of: should we just take this and then verbatim apply it, which is what many groups do, or should we think about the rationale? And my position is that both of these groups are, alhamdulillah, respected 'ulama, and that we should at least allow them to discuss and engage.

The main issue comes (unfortunately, and I am opposed to this) in that one of these two strands, one of these two paradigms, has essentially taken over, or eclipsed, if you like, the fatwa scene, and especially social media, especially Islam websites that are answering Q&A about Islam. These types of websites, they give positions that are respected in their own mind. But what has happened is that a very literal sense comes that does not allow for any type of thinking through, any type of rationale. And in fact, even some of the scholars of that trend themselves have criticized others. One of my own teachers, Shaykh Ibn Uthaymin, Allah yarhamuh, would say many times, he would publicly complain about the rise of literalism (it's called dhahiriyya), the rise of literalism and the diminishing of fiqh, of understanding.

And the problem comes: the issue is not that one group holds this. The issue is that, unlike the Sahaba, who allowed for two opinions, this group does not allow the possibility of any other view being legitimate. And this is really the problem: the problem of intolerance, the problem of "if you don't agree with my literalism, you are rejecting the Sunnah, you are against the Sunnah, and therefore you are somebody who is going to be doomed," or la'natullah, or something of this nature.

And another major problem that comes is that this group, even though they're small and they're relatively modern, despite the fact they claim to go back to the earliest of times, the fact is that undeniably they jump over, they bypass 14 centuries of scholarship, and they restrict the understanding of Islam to a small group of modern scholars of one particular land, of one particular mindset, that are self-replicating their own views over and over again. And the problem is not in them holding the views; that's perfectly fine. The problem is them imposing that one view on the entire globe, such that anybody who contradicts their narrative is deemed to be somebody who is, a'udhu billah, against the Sunnah of the Prophet ﷺ. And this is extremism, and this is a type of narrow-mindedness and dangerous mentality that in fact does cause a fanaticism, and it does lead to many problems of the Ummah.

And the net result, therefore, of all of this is that you do get a group of people that are very literalist, very committed and dedicated to the interpretations of their 'ulama, and anybody who disagrees with them is deemed to be not worthy of their love or attention. And this is not good for the Ummah. And one of the main points in me going into this detail and talking about all of this, and in fact my entire philosophy when I do these Q&As, is to preach tolerance and respect of our tradition. I might have my views, and maybe I'll try to prove my views with passion, but if respected 'ulama have other views, alhamdulillah, no problem. That's their method in ijtihad, and Allah 'azza wa jal will reward them for their sincerity.

Now, all of this was a prelude to this question, because again, you have to understand that this group of scholars, because of socio-political factors, economic factors, they do dominate the waves, if you like. They dominate social media, they have influenced modern discourse, to the point that many Muslims don't really even know that this is a very small minority, and we have, alhamdulillah, a very beautiful heritage and history of Islamic scholarship. So today I will demonstrate for you that in fact there have been diverse opinions from the very beginning of time, and the greatest 'ulama have actually given exceptions to this hadith. It's nothing that is new that is coming here.

So we look first and foremost at the evidence and how it was understood in the earliest of times. Now, in this particular case, Ibn Mas'ud, the one who narrated the hadith, it is very clear that he would not allow his own women to practice these types of things. And so he was of those basically saying: the hadith says it, let's just practice it. Interestingly enough, Aisha, our mother, she's also one of the narrators of this hadith, in one of the versions. And yet we have reported from her that she would allow women to pluck hair from their faces.

So again, very interesting over here. It is reported in a number of early books, including the Kitab of Abu Yusuf, the student of Abu Hanifa, and also Ibn Battal, the commentary of al-Bukhari, mentions this: that Abu Ishaq mentions that my wife visited Aisha and she asked her (and my wife was a lady who loved to beautify herself). So Abu Ishaq is narrating this: my wife was a lady who loved to beautify herself. We were newly married, she's a young lady, she wants to beautify herself. And she asked Aisha, "Is it permissible for a woman to pluck her eyebrows?" And Aisha, our mother, says, "You may remove anything that irritates you," you don't like it, "as much as you want." You may beautify yourself as much as you want.

It is also reported in the Musannaf of 'Abd al-Razzaq that a woman was with Aisha radiAllahu 'anha and she said, "O Umm al-Mu'minin, O Mother of the Believers, there are hairs in my face that I don't like. May I pluck them in order to beautify myself for my husband?" And Aisha once again said to her, "You may get rid of anything that irritates you, and prepare for your husband as you prepare when guests come to visit you." When other ladies come and you make yourself look good, so then you should prepare yourself for your husband as well. In other words, when you have visitors and guests coming, ladies are coming to visit you, then you will look dignified and nice and whatnot. So Aisha radiAllahu 'anha is saying that, yes, of course you make yourself look good and you beautify yourself for your husband.

Now, here we have, if you like, two different paradigms from the very beginning: that Ibn Mas'ud would not allow his own wives to do any of these things, and he is taking basically the literal version, which is completely allowed. As we said, this is something that does exist from the time of the Sahaba. And we have Aisha radiAllahu 'anha (and she is the lady, by the way, and she should know better, and the rulings are pertaining to her, radiAllahu 'anha) that she is giving this fatwa. The lady is literally saying, "I want to basically shave off or trim my eyebrows; am I allowed to do that?" And she is saying, "You may do that." So we find this tension, if you like. Again, there was no tension between Aisha and Ibn Mas'ud, but I'm saying the tension in understanding this narration.

Also, from the earliest of times, a number of our scholars were wondering about the hadith here. We do need to think about this. Overall, let's say if the hadith had not come about eyebrows, generally speaking, nobody would assume this to be a sin. You beautify yourself. A woman is allowed to shave any body hair she wants to. In fact, she is mandated to shave, as you know, certain parts of her body, the man and the woman, and she may keep her hair as long or as short as she wants. She may put on any type of bangles or beautification for her husband, dress up for her husband.

So the question about the la'na of Allah coming upon something like an eyebrow: generally speaking, Allah's la'na is a very, very big deal. Allah's la'na is huge. Allah 'azza wa jal, His la'na is upon those who reject Him. His la'na is upon the idol worshippers. His la'na is upon the one who murders; it's in the Qur'an, that the one who murders, Allah's la'na is on him. So if you look at the sins that Allah has given the la'na, these are major sins. Now, to add eyebrows to the list, one wonders what is going on.

And I'm not the first one to wonder. You have, for example, the famous, great 'alim al-Qarafi, one of the great 'ulama of the Maliki madhhab. He writes in his book al-Dhakhira, he mentions this hadith, and he says that, "I haven't seen the scholars of the Malikis and the Shafi'is discussing the reasons or the causes of why there is la'na in this situation. I don't understand why." Because he says that, "I understand that if this is a woman who is deceiving other people, in order to basically pretend that she is somebody that's more beautiful than she is when the suitor comes, when somebody proposes for her, then I understand. However, if it is for the wife, for her husband, then there is no deception going on." And so he's questioning that: what is this? How can we understand the la'na?

And another great scholar of our tradition, the great mufassir Ibn 'Ashur: Ibn 'Ashur wrote one of the most original and amazing commentaries of the Qur'an, called al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir. Ibn 'Ashur writes that, as for this hadith of Allah's la'na on these categories of women, he says it is something that is difficult to interpret or understand, like, I don't understand why there's la'na on these things. And he says the only interpretation that I find to be reasonable is that these characteristics were the characteristics of the ladies of ill repute, i.e. the prostitutes of that time, and they would use these characteristics to advertise their profession that way. And the famous scholar Ibn 'Ashur, he says that even if the Shari'ah were to forbid these things for whatever reasons, it should not reach the level of la'n in and of itself. This is Ibn 'Ashur saying here.

So he is basically saying that the reason why these things have been prohibited is that in those days, when a lady practiced that evil profession, in order to advertise that she is that type of lady, she would have certain characteristics. And of them is that she would remove her eyebrows, let's say, or of them is that she would do the other things mentioned in this hadith. And therefore it now makes sense: Allah's la'na is on those ladies that are selling themselves to these men, because obviously that is destroying society, destroying the moral fabric of society. Now we understand the la'na coming, because the la'na is not on plucking a hair; the la'na will be on the women that are doing that for the sake of this evil profession.

So this is something that Tahir ibn 'Ashur says. And Ibn al-Jawzi also mentions a similar comment; the famous Hanbali scholar Ibn al-Jawzi, he also mentions something similar in this regard. And therefore we find these 'ulama, they're trying to rationalize: why is this thing prohibited? Again, like Ibn 'Ashur said, if Allah had made it haram, we understand, okay, it's haram. It's His right to make it haram; nobody can question. But then one wonders: something like this, to have the la'na on it? What is causing the la'na? That must be something more than just plucking the eyebrow. And that's why these 'ulama say that the interpretation is that the la'na was for this profession, and these characteristics were symbolic of that profession. This makes a lot of sense.

Now, what did the fuqaha, what did the scholars of fiqh say about this issue of women plucking their eyebrows? Well, again, the madhahib have differed over this issue. And yes, there is no question that many 'ulama took this hadith and they considered it to be copy and paste, and literal, and they said, khalas, this is what it is. And there's no problem with that opinion. And as I will conclude, there is no doubt that that is the safer opinion. There is no doubt that you're getting out of any controversy. But there have been alternative voices from the very beginning of time. Our mother Aisha is the first one to set this entire paradigm, and are we going to accuse her of not following the Sunnah in this regard? And again, the point being that we have this controversy from the very beginning of time. Even if you don't agree with it, at least respect it. At least know that it exists, and understand that there are many 'ulama who have held the other view.

In fact, the great scholar Imam Ahmad, he had a very interesting view in this regard. Imam Ahmad said that what is prohibited is the plucking of the eyebrow. In his opinion, he said if a woman shaves it (or later Hanbali scholars said if she dyes it, for example, such that it's no longer seen), then it would be permissible. So Imam Ahmad was asked about this, as al-Khallal says in Kitab al-Wuquf wa al-Tarajjul min Masa'il al-Imam Ahmad, that Imam Ahmad was asked, "Should a lady remove the hair of her eyebrows?" And Imam Ahmad said, "I don't like that she plucks it, but I don't have a problem if she shaves it." This is the Imam of the school. Many of the later people who follow this Imam in our times, they disagree, or they don't mention this very fatwa from Imam Ahmad himself.

And other great Hanbali scholars even allowed more than this. Of course Ibn Qudamah, the famous, great author of al-Mughni, Ibn Qudamah also mentions that the prohibition in the hadith is for plucking, not for shaving.

By the way, I have to make the disclaimer here that we're talking about just the eyebrows. As for any other facial hair, there should be no problem with that. So if there's any hair growing (because it is not the natural default of a woman to grow hair in the chin area or above the lips or whatnot), that hair, of course, it can be removed. The hadith comes about the namisat, and the interpretation is that nams is to remove the hair, to pluck the hair of the eyebrows. That's how Imam Ahmad understood it: that the prohibition is to pluck the hair. And he goes, this is a type of, basically, mutilation, and he allowed the shaving of it. Now, this is Imam Ahmad's position.

Some Hanbali 'ulama actually allowed for more than this, and of them is the great 'alim and the shaykh and the zahid and the saint, 'Abd al-Qadir al-Jilani. You've all heard of 'Abd al-Qadir al-Jilani. What many people do not know was that he was a great 'alim, and he was a Hanbali as well. And in his Ghunyah, he says that as for the lady, then the madhhab basically is that she should not remove her eyebrows, she should not shape her eyebrows. And then he says: and others have argued that it is allowed for the lady who is married to shape her eyebrows for her husband, if her husband wants her to do that, and also if she feels that if she doesn't do so, then her husband might turn away from her, or find interest in maybe another marriage or something, and she's going to have issues or problems. In this case, he says, it is allowed for her to beautify herself by shaping her eyebrows, because there is a clear benefit to be gained over here.

Just like (this is still 'Abd al-Qadir al-Jilani) it is allowed for her to wear beautiful clothing and to wear good perfume and to wear the most expensive garments or finery or whatnot, and to be playful and to be jesting and joking with her husband. All of these are encouraged for her. And therefore, listen to 'Abd al-Qadir al-Jilani: the la'n in the hadith is for the ladies that are doing it for prostitution, for other men to come to them that are not their husbands.

Notice, this is the rationale we talked about from the time of the Sahaba, with the prayer of 'Asr: looking at the reasoning and then saying, okay, the reasoning is the prostitution. And therefore, when it's not done for that, because it's no longer a sign (that was something that was a sign back then; these days, as you are aware, it is no longer a sign just for one class of ladies), 'Abd al-Qadir al-Jilani says if a woman does it for her husband, the la'na cannot be upon this lady.

And it's not just 'Abd al-Qadir al-Jilani. One of the greatest Hanbali 'ulama of his era, the great 'alim and the great scholar Ibn al-Jawzi, he also has this same position. In fact, you should know Ibn al-Jawzi actually has the largest book ever written in the Hanbali school about women overall. He has Ahkam al-Nisa', the rulings about women. It's like 400, 500 volumes, the edition that I have. And it's all about the rulings of women and the blessings of women and how to treat women, the hadith about women. It's a very interesting book. And he himself has a section, obviously, in this book about this hadith.

And again, I ask those brothers that, in their eagerness, want to just refute by quoting some modern scholars of one land: would you consider Ibn al-Jawzi to be somebody who rejects hadith, to be somebody who's a modernist or progressive? This is Ibn al-Jawzi. Ibn al-Jawzi writes this, listen to this: that the apparent meaning of these ahadith seems to be that the prohibition of these things is unconditional. That's the apparent meaning, he says; it's very clear. And that unconditional understanding is what Ibn Mas'ud himself derived from this. So he admits there is an opinion out there, and that opinion is that there are no circumstances where this is allowed, and that's Ibn Mas'ud's view. Excellent.

Then he goes: and it is also possible to interpret this hadith in one of three ways. Okay, there's another opinion as well. This is Ibn al-Jawzi. The first of them: that this was a sign for prostitutes. This is Ibn al-Jawzi saying, kana min shi'ar al-fajirat, this was a sign for those that are seeking to seduce men. So the la'na is for them, not for the action, but for the lifestyle, what they are doing. Number one.

Number two, he goes, one can also interpret that this is for ladies (now again, you have to remember, back then the veil, sometimes even the face covering, would be put on, and so women, when they're single, they might want to portray themselves to be other than how they look). And so the second is that there is a type of deception that is being done. The lady should be who she is. When the suitor comes to see whether he wants to propose or not, the both of them should know how they are. So this is the second thing, that there is a type of deception. He goes, that is also not allowed.

Number three, he said, is for the tattoos: that there is a permanent change to the creation of Allah, like in the tattoos. This has nothing to do with the thing here. So he goes, as for the eyebrow thing, we must interpret it: the hadith of the plucking of the eyebrows, we should understand it in one of the first two categories. Either it was meant for women of ill repute, or it was meant for those that are trying to deceive a suitor when they are single, and they want to deceive somebody that they look different than they actually look.

Then Ibn al-Jawzi says: my own teacher, al-Anmati, he would say (and this is the Hanbali madhhab), he would say that if a lady takes from the hair of her face in order to beautify herself for her husband, there is no problem with that. The problem comes when a person comes to propose and he doesn't know what the lady looks like (they might be covering or whatnot) and she tries to deceive him in that manner. That would be problematic. Now again, this is Ibn al-Jawzi. What are you going to do about this great scholar, Ibn al-Jawzi? That is in the Hanbali madhhab.

The Shafi'i school is much more explicit. Actually, this is the fatwa of the Shafi'i school. The Shafi'i school, they understood this hadith, by and large, to apply to single ladies that are trying to deceive or trying to portray themselves other than they are. They explicitly allowed married ladies to beautify themselves for their husbands, and they said this is of the goals of the Shari'ah. Why wouldn't we want a lady to beautify herself for her husband? And one of the great icons of the Shafi'i school, al-Mawardi, who died 450 Hijrah (of course, he is the author of al-Hawi al-Kabir, one of the encyclopedias of Shafi'i fiqh), he explicitly says that if a lady does this to beautify herself for her husband, this is not haram. Why? He says the woman is required, she is obliged, to beautify herself for her husband.

This was also the position of Imam al-Ghazali, also of the Shafi'i scholars, the famous al-Ghazali, and other scholars as well. Now again, you will find some of the Shafi'i madhhab that did not allow this, so that's fine as well, but this is the default of the position. And in fact al-Hafidh Ibn Hajar himself, the great Shafi'i authority, in the Fath al-Bari, he basically says that if the husband allows this and approves this, then it is something that is allowed to do. Therefore you now have the Shafi'i madhhab as well allowing this.

And as for the Malikis, again, you have a number of Malikis allowing this as well. Al-Qadi 'Iyad, he himself mentions the narration of Aisha about this issue of allowing some people to pluck. And the Maliki scholar al-'Adawi, he says in Kifayat al-Talib that this prohibition will apply only to those ladies who are not allowed to beautify themselves. So women who are married to their husbands, they are obliged to beautify; that narration will not apply to them.

Now, the same applies in the Hanafi school. You will find a number of authorities (again, the Fatawa Hindiyyah of the Hanafi school) that allow the married lady to beautify herself for her husband in this regard. And yes, you will find some Hanafis who also follow Ibn Mas'ud's fatwa that doesn't allow it unconditionally.

Now therefore, to conclude, I will quote you the modern encyclopedia, al-Mawsu'ah al-Fiqhiyyah, which is a modern encyclopedia written by a group of 'ulama. In volume 15, page 69, they say the majority of scholars have opined that this prohibition of the hadith is not universal, it's not unconditional. And Ibn Mas'ud and al-Tabari and others, they said it is unconditional, and they said that it is haram in all circumstances. However, the majority said that it is not allowed for a single lady to beautify herself in this regard. As for the married lady, or any lady that requires it (if some type of issue has happened, medical issue or whatnot), then there is no problem in her doing that. And they say this is the jumhur al-fuqaha: the majority of scholars have allowed this, because the lady is required, or obliged, to beautify herself for her husband.

Therefore, to conclude this first question, to conclude all of this, we state: the concept of beautification overall is something that, without a doubt, is allowed for a lady within the confines of the Shari'ah. And to beautify herself for her husband is one of the most important characteristics of women. They want to beautify themselves, and they should beautify themselves. And the goals of the Shari'ah would indicate that a woman is beautiful for her husband, and the husband is looking good for his wife and taking care of her. The two of them should have that love and that care and that comfort with each other.

Now, the Shari'ah of course has prohibited certain types of things that are haram. Obviously you cannot do things that would be permanent, such as a tattoo, because that's a complete change. However, generally speaking, a woman's personal preferences of hair and makeup and jewelry and clothing and style, generally speaking, the Shari'ah is silent on that. And so the Shari'ah has allowed the lady to dress up, especially in the privacy of her house, in a manner that is pleasing to her husband, and vice versa: the husband should do the same.

Now, this hadith comes along, and our scholars from the very beginning of time, al-Khattabi, Ibn al-Jawzi and Tahir ibn 'Ashur, they're trying to understand. Even if sometimes we don't understand Allah's wisdom, that's definitely not a problem. We don't know why we do tawaf seven times; we just say sami'na wa ata'na. Totally understandable. But here we have something where, as our scholars say, when the reward or the punishment doesn't fit the crime, we have to think a little bit more. Why would the la'na come on plucking some hair from the face? And that question has been asked by many great 'ulama of the past, and the response seems to be very obvious to many 'ulama (I just quoted you some of them in today's lecture), and that is that the la'na, or the curse of Allah, was not on the action of plucking the eyebrow. It was on its association with that lifestyle that was well known, and everybody who did that was known to be of those who practiced that lifestyle, and that's why the la'na came. Now, that makes complete sense.

Therefore, when the cause does not exist anymore, when a lady is doing it not for that reason, and she's doing it in a halal manner to satisfy her husband, does the same ruling apply? This is where we now see so many great 'ulama have a difference of opinion. And we have the Shafi'i madhhab, and we have Ibn al-Jawzi, and we have al-Qadi 'Iyad of the Malikis, and we have some of the Ahnaf, and we have Imam Ahmad himself. To be clear, as I said, Imam Ahmad allowed the shaving. So again, if you want to be Hanbali, then you may follow that position: don't pluck it, shave it. You will get the same thing done. His point was just: we don't know why; Allah has cursed the plucking, so then don't pluck, but do anything else that you want. So again, if you wanted to follow that position.

Now, the other position, which is Ibn Mas'ud's position, is of course dominant in one strand of modern Islam that claims to follow the Salaf. And that's not a problem. There's no problem following that strand or that interpretation, because Ibn Mas'ud was also the one who followed it. My issue, or my complaint, or my criticism, is in the condemnation of the other opinion as having no merit whatsoever. And this is the problem of, basically, fanaticism and intolerance. I've just quoted you great 'ulama from the past. These were not modern people who are liberal and Western, or taking from the kuffar, or America or England. These are great 'ulama: Ibn al-Jawzi, as I said, from within the Hanbali tradition, and all of these 'ulama.

And again, as usual, this is a smaller lecture, and so, bottom line: **if you wish to follow the Shafi'i position, and many other 'ulama, for the married lady to beautify herself for the sake of her husband, then inshaAllah you have great precedent, and there should be no problem in that.** And if you wanted to follow the more conservative opinion, and you wish to be on the safer side and err on the side of caution, and follow Ibn Mas'ud's position in this regard rather than Aisha's position, you definitely have precedent, and again, there's no problem in doing that. But respect the other position. Understand the other position is there.

Now, that having been said, **none of the scholars allowed it for the lady that was not doing it for her husband.** So please understand this point. Let us stick with our tradition and not completely change it for absolutely no reason. None of the scholars allowed it for the lady to beautify herself for people that are not basically her husband. So you understand this point here: we're not going to open that door. We're talking about married women beautifying themselves for their husbands; then, inshaAllah, there is concession from the time of Aisha. And other than that, definitely we should stick with the traditions as much as possible. And Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala knows best.
